extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students (practitioners in patent litigation)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and equitable criteria courts apply when deciding whether to grant or refuse preliminary (temporary) injunctions in patent infringement cases, including defendant good faith, plaintiff conduct, patent validity doubts, public interest, and balance of hardships. Covers reissues, prior patents/uses, laches/acquiescence, and related equitable defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches / Unreasonable Delay by Plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay by the plaintiff in prosecuting a suit (e.g., permitting a suit to remain three years unprosecuted) may bar an injunction; patentees should not be forced to institute proceedings as soon as infringement is ascertained or lose protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider hardship to patentees from immediate suit requirement and whether defendant is responsible; examples include Hockholzer v. Eager and New Home Sewing Mach. Co. (1883). Delay may be treated as laches when defendant is prejudiced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's Violation of Equitable Obligations to Defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff has violated equitable obligations (express or implied contract) toward the defendant and thereby placed the defendant in a position where self-preservation compelled infringement, the injunction will be denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a licensor secretly underselling a licensee, granting licenses at lower royalties, or other conduct that renders court interference unjust (cases cited in text). Acts of bad faith toward the public may also justify denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent Conduct by Plaintiff (Denial of Injunction)
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will be denied where the plaintiff has acted fraudulently toward the defendant (e.g., secretly undersold his licensees or fraudulently licensed others), or where the application is for purposes of coercion or extortion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific case citations (Washburn & Moen Mfg. Co. v. Scutt; Hoffheins v. Brandt) and examples emphasize courts’ refusal to aid a plaintiff who has misled parties or injured defendant's trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release of Past Liability Does Not Bar Future Injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: The release of an infringer from liability for past infringement is not a bar to an injunction for future infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Release for past acts does not preclude equitable relief prohibiting future infringing acts (see Babcock & Wilcox v. Pioneer Iron Works (1888)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant Misled by Plaintiff May Still Be Enjoined
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if defendant was misled by plaintiff into believing his present acts did not infringe, the defendant may still be enjoined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as Sarven v. Hall show misrepresentation to defendant does not automatically prevent injunction if equities otherwise favor plaintiff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable Defenses Where Plaintiff Also Breached Contract
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction may be refused if the plaintiff has violated a contract with the defendant, even when the defendant has also broken the contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts weigh the equitable conduct of both parties (e.g., Crowell v. Parmenter (1878)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper Purpose in Seeking Injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff’s main object in seeking an injunction is improper — to compel the defendant to act or refrain from acting in other matters, or to enforce recognition of rights from third parties — the court will ordinarily refuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An injunction is to preserve existing rights, not to punish past injuries or indirectly prejudice the defendant by placing him within the plaintiff’s power (discussion in §1196; cases: Poppenhusen v. N.T. Gutta Percha Comb Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of Injunction: Preserve Rights, Prevent Future Injury
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction is remedial, intended to prevent future injuries and multiplicity of suits, not to punish past wrongs or to force compromise of litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will not grant injunctive relief merely to stop litigation or to obtain litigation advantages (cited authorities: Cook v. Ernest; Poppenhusen, Morris v. Lowell Mfg. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant’s Good Faith and Honest Belief
rubrics_metrics.description: defendant’s good faith (honest belief that device is different or ignorance of patent) may weigh against granting a preliminary injunction, particularly if defendant entered into important contracts or invested large capital that would suffer if business interrupted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere innocence does not guarantee avoidance of relief, but good faith plus potential severe prejudice and ability to protect plaintiff by other means can lead to withholding injunction. (See §1197 and examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of Hardships / Serious Prejudice to Defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: Where defendant would be seriously injured by an injunction (e.g., large investments, ruin of enterprise, essential part of wider process), courts may withhold an injunction or except contracts from its operation provided defendant tenders compensation or is responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts weigh whether injury to defendant would be out of proportion to plaintiff’s benefit and may allow continued use to fulfil contracts (see examples and discussion in §1200).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant’s Patent or Acting Under Patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If defendant owns or acts under a patent that on its face authorizes the use of the process/device, an injunction may be withheld until final hearing; a defendant’s patent raises doubts about identity or priority and is evidence of good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant’s patent is prima facie relevant and entitled to consideration unless evidently void; may prevent interim relief until comparison of specifications (see §1198 and cases like Goodyear v. Dunbar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Use / Employment Before Plaintiff’s Patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant will not be enjoined from using an invention which he employed before the plaintiff’s patent was granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior use is a recognized defense; cases such as Dorian v. Gnie are cited where prior employment justifies withholding injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant Holds Patent for Same Invention (Prima Facie Valid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where defendant has a patent for the same invention that is prima facie valid, an injunction will be refused while the courts compare the two specifications to determine identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant’s patent is proof that Patent Office experts regarded it as substantially different; it shows good faith and militate against harsh remedies (text cites Westlake v. Garter, Blanchard v. Putman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant’s Patent for an Improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant who holds a patent for an improvement is not necessarily sheltered from injunction if the infringement of the plaintiff’s valid claims is clear; the improvement patent does not avail him beyond its proper scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An improvement patent may limit defendant’s exposure only to its scope; clear infringement of plaintiff’s claims can still justify injunction (examples: Morse Fountain Pen Co. v. Esterbrook Steel Pen Mfg. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: When Defendant Operates Under Other Patents in Full Competition
rubrics_metrics.description: No injunction will be granted where defendant openly uses a device made under other patents in full competition and in good faith, unless the injury is irreparable or defendant cannot respond in damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may require special showing of irreparable harm to plaintiff or inability to compensate (cases: Burleigh Rock Drill Co. v. Lobdell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference/Adverse Titles / Patent Office Proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction may be granted against a defeated party in an interference if former relies on his own prior patent; injunctions are refused where adverse titles are still undetermined in the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Patent Office contests or interferences are pending, courts are cautious — may refuse interim relief if titles unresolved (see Greenwood v. Bracher; National Feather Duster Co. v. Dearborn Duster Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court Doubts as to Validity, Title, or Infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where, notwithstanding plaintiff’s evidence, the court is still in doubt about the patent’s validity, title, or the allegation of infringement, the injunction may be denied and rights left unchanged until final hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary motions should establish a case requiring prevention of irreparable injury; otherwise injunction withheld (Sickels v. Young, Isaacs v. Cooper).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Recent, Specification Obscure, or Proof Meagre
rubrics_metrics.description: No injunction will issue where a patent is recent, the specification obscure, novelty denied, or the proof of infringement meagre — at least until adequate investigation or final hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require reliable prior adjudication or sufficient opportunity to investigate patentability before granting interim relief (multiple cited cases; §1199 discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue Patents: Expanded Claims and Delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Injunctions on re-issues are governed by whether the re-issue attempts to extend the original scope, whether the re-issue is broader, or whether the re-issue was delayed (e.g., ten years) with disputed validity; courts may refuse interim relief in such circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where valid re-issue claims are infringed, injunctions can issue; but where breadth or timing of re-issue creates doubt, relief may be withheld (cases: Brewster v. Parry; Starrett v. Athol Mach. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on Public Interest and Third Parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts consider probable effect of an injunction on public interests or third parties; injunction may be refused where it would be injurious to public or where public acquiescence favors defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include refusal where an injunction would cause great hardship to public or where other orders exist; courts balance public consequences (see §1200 and cited cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of Suits / Preventing Repeated Infringements
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction is intended to prevent multiplicity of suits or repeated infringements; it is not to be used to cause litigation or force a settlement, and is not warranted when its object is to establish apparent title against all users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts refuse injunctions sought to establish blanket claims to induce payments from all users (Western Union Tel. Co. v. Balt. & Ohio Tel. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence, Licenses, and Royalty History
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive licensing, payment of royalties, or public acquiescence in the plaintiff’s title may support or affect entitlement to an injunction; conversely, where plaintiff has been guilty of laches or sold licenses and defendant is responsible, injunction may be refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License history and whether royalties or license-fees were paid influence equilibrium; long delay with no action can defeat interim relief (examples throughout text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Conduct: Maker/Seller vs Mere User
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction is more readily issued against a maker-seller (who makes and sells infringing articles) than against a mere user; if the defendant makes and sells, the wrong is increasing and weighs toward granting relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider whether defendant’s activity is a growing commercial injury versus passive use (cited cases: Morris v. Lowell Mfg. Co.; Covert v. Curtis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of Adequate Alternative Remedies / Uselessness to Plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: If an injunction would be useless to plaintiff (e.g., other effective orders exist) or other adequate remedies are equally available, courts may withhold injunctive relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An injunction should not be granted where other remedies would prevent the injury or where granting would be inequitable given other available relief (see cases in §1200).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Openly Defective or Clearly Void
rubrics_metrics.description: No injunction will be granted where the patent is openly defective, evidently void, or has glaring defects such that court can entertain no doubt as to its invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where defects are manifest, it would be unjust to restrain defendant from using machinery constructed at great expense (Isaacs v. Cooper and related authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: When Plaintiff’s Title is Only Equitable and Being Litigated Elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: If plaintiff claims only an equitable title which is being contested in local courts, a federal court may decline to issue an injunction in the patent suit pending resolution of local litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts avoid interfering with state court determinations of equitable title (see Continental Store Service Co. v. New York Store Service Co.).
